name: sglang

facts.description: SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models and multimodal models.

title: SGLang: A High-Performance Serving Framework for LLMs and Multimodal Models
answer: SGLang is an open-source, Apache-2.0 licensed serving framework for large language and multimodal models, written in Python and hosted on GitHub. It sits in the inference and deployment layer of the AI stack, turning trained models into responsive services from a single GPU to distributed clusters. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it is built for production-grade throughput and memory control, with features like disaggregated prefill/decode and speculative decoding, rather than for quick prototyping.

sections.body: SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models and multimodal models, developed by the SGLang project and released under the Apache-2.0 licence. Its official website describes it as supporting deployment from a single GPU to distributed clusters. It first appeared as an open-source project and has since become a widely used inference engine, with the GitHub repository showing 36,751 stars as of the facts. In the AI stack, it occupies the serving and inference layer: it takes trained models and runs them efficiently to answer requests, rather than handling training or data preparation. The homepage lists recent release notes and model support, and the framework incorporates disaggregated prefill/decode, speculative decoding, parallelisms, a zero-overhead scheduler, and optimized GPU kernels.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: SGLang is used for serving large language and multimodal models in production, including text generation, reasoning, coding, vision, and agentic tasks. Its model catalogue lists a wide range of architectures, from dense and Mixture-of-Experts models to multimodal and speech-to-speech systems, with context windows up to 1M tokens. It is strongest where high throughput and low latency matter, such as online inference for chat, agents, and document understanding. The site highlights optimizations for prefill and decode, including kernel-level work that raised DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash decode throughput from 35 to 873 tokens per second on specific hardware. It also supports diffusion models through SGLang-Diffusion, as shown in an integration with NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 for robot manipulation evaluation. For training or fine-tuning, SGLang is not the primary tool; it focuses on inference and serving.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Learning SGLang requires a working knowledge of Python, since the framework is written in Python, and familiarity with deep learning concepts such as transformer architectures, attention, and quantization. The official site offers a model catalogue, blog posts with detailed technical explanations, and release notes, but it does not present a structured beginner tutorial. A developer new to model serving may need to understand GPU memory management, parallelism strategies, and inference optimization to use advanced features effectively. The site's blog posts assume some systems knowledge, discussing CUDA graphs, kernel fusion, and KV cache layouts. For a student, the material is accessible if they already know Python and have trained or run a model before, but the site does not provide a step-by-step introduction to serving.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: SGLang integrates with popular model formats and libraries, including Hugging Face models, as shown by the RLinf integration that treats Cosmos3 as an external Hugging Face model through an adapter layer. It supports NVIDIA GPUs and technologies such as FlashInfer, DeepEP, and NIXL, and works with frameworks like FSDP2 for training. The official site lists a broad model catalogue covering many open-source and proprietary architectures, and the GitHub repository has a large community with 36,751 stars. Documentation includes release notes, technical blog posts, and a model catalogue, though the site does not describe a formal community forum or support channels. The first SGLang Summit is announced for November 12 to 13, 2026, in San Francisco, indicating an active community.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: SGLang is built primarily for production performance rather than quick prototyping. Its homepage emphasizes features like disaggregated prefill/decode, speculative decoding, parallelisms, a zero-overhead scheduler, and optimized GPU kernels, all aimed at maximizing throughput and minimizing latency in deployment. The blog posts detail kernel-level optimizations and memory savings, such as reducing KV cache size and improving decode throughput. However, the site also mentions a CPU-only simulator that runs the real scheduler and caches with a latency predictor, which can help with planning and testing without a GPU. For rapid experiments, a developer might find lighter frameworks easier, but SGLang's focus on performance means it may require more setup and tuning. The cost is complexity: many optimizations are opt-in flags, and the site does not claim to be a simple prototyping tool.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: SGLang is used in industry for serving large models, as evidenced by its integration with NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 and support for models from major developers like DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi. The site's model catalogue and blog posts show active day-0 support for new architectures, suggesting it is a current standard for high-performance inference. The GitHub repository has 36,751 stars, indicating significant adoption. For someone choosing it for work, SGLang skills are relevant for roles in ML engineering, inference optimization, and MLOps, particularly where large-scale deployment is needed. The site does not provide specific career information or job market data, so claims about demand should be based on its visible ecosystem and adoption. It is not described as a legacy choice; the frequent updates and summit suggest it is actively developed.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: SGLang is typically used with Python and integrates with the broader Python AI ecosystem, including PyTorch, Hugging Face, and NVIDIA libraries like FlashInfer and DeepEP. It serves models that are often trained with frameworks such as FSDP2, as shown in the RLinf integration. In a polyglot pattern, SGLang handles the inference serving layer, while training and data processing may happen in other frameworks. It can be deployed alongside orchestration tools and APIs, and its /v1/responses endpoint suggests compatibility with OpenAI-style interfaces. The site does not list specific competing frameworks, but its role is as a specialized serving runtime that can sit behind application backends, not as a general-purpose ML library.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: SGLang is weak at training and fine-tuning, which are outside its scope as a serving framework. Some features are immature or changing, such as the CPU-only simulator that predicts TTFT within about 6% on most traces but up to 10% on the longest 32K to 128K traces, and the /v1/responses endpoint that no longer retains results in memory unless the server starts with --enable-response-store. The site does not say how easy it is to install on non-NVIDIA hardware, nor does it provide a clear comparison with other serving frameworks. The official material does not state the minimum hardware requirements or the level of support for Windows or macOS. Many optimizations are opt-in and may require specific library versions, such as FlashInfer 0.6.18 for MXFP4 experts on Hopper. The site also does not address security or multi-tenancy concerns for production deployments.
